questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: The assumed reader of a procedure
questions.learningObjective: identify what a guide's opening sentences fix about its reader
questions.stem: A bicycle repair sheet opens: 'Some riders find the rear wheel awkward to reach. Everything below assumes a bike fitted with a rim brake and a bottle cage; bikes with a hydraulic disc brake are covered on a separate sheet.' What has the sheet settled about the reader it is written for?

options.text: Which kind of bike the sheet applies to, so the reader can tell at once if it is the right instructions
How much experience the reader has, since the warning about the wheel shows a beginner is assumed
options.misconception: reads a remark about one part being awkward as proof that the reader is a beginner

options.text: What job the reader does for a living, since only workshop staff would follow these steps
options.misconception: supplies a job role that the sheet never names anywhere in its opening

options.text: How many repairs the reader has attempted before, since the sheet is clearly written for a first attempt
options.misconception: treats a note about which brake type fits as a statement about the reader's experience

questions.explanation: A guide fixes its reader mainly by narrowing the range of objects it speaks for, and this sheet does that in its second sentence: rim brake, bottle cage, everything else on another sheet. That is a statement about which machine the steps will fit, and a reader with a disc-brake bike learns immediately to stop looking. The opening sentence is about a physical fact, that the rear wheel is hard to reach, and it is aimed at riders who have already been riding; it says nothing about skill. Nothing in either sentence names a job or counts past repairs, so those are inferences the reader supplies rather than things the sheet has settled.
questions.hint: Look for the sentence that narrows what the steps will fit.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: Prerequisite stated before the first step
questions.learningObjective: find the setup a numbered procedure assumes but never supplies
questions.stem: A card for growing cress reads in full: '1. Scatter the seed evenly over the compost. 2. Keep the compost damp, not wet. 3. Seedlings appear in five to seven days.' What is the card missing?

options.text: A note about which seed to buy, since cress sold for sprouting will not behave as the card says
options.misconception: supplies a buying detail the card never turns on, when the gap is in the setup the card itself names

options.text: The step that puts compost in a tray, since step 1 scatters seed onto something the card never provides
A daily quantity of water, since damp is not a measure and a reader cannot repeat it exactly
options.misconception: treats damp as the defect, when the card's first step depends on compost that no step supplies

options.text: A step for thinning the seedlings, since a crowded tray produces weak growth and the card stops too early
options.misconception: asks for a step beyond what the card claims to cover, since it ends at germination

questions.explanation: The test for a missing setup is whether an earlier step refers to something the guide has not yet produced. Step 1 scatters seed over the compost, so the compost has to be in a container before step 1 begins, and nothing between the title and step 1 puts it there. That makes the first numbered step unperformable as printed, which is a harder fault than an inexact quantity. The card does state a stopping point, seedling appearance, so a thinning step would be a suggestion for a stage it explicitly does not cover, and damp versus wet is a contrast the card does supply rather than a gap it leaves.
questions.hint: Check the nouns each step depends on and see whether an earlier step creates them.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: The failure point a step does not mention
questions.learningObjective: locate the point in a step where the reader is exposed to a risk the step never names

stimulus.body: Removing the rear wheel. 1. Shift to the smallest sprocket. 2. Open the brake quick release. 3. Loosen the axle nuts by hand, then lift the wheel out of the dropouts.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A repair sheet reads: 'Removing the rear wheel. 1. Shift to the smallest sprocket. 2. Open the brake quick release. 3. Loosen the axle nuts by hand, then lift the wheel out of the dropouts.' Which risk does step 3 hand the reader without warning?

options.text: The brake pads pick up chain oil while the wheel is out and stop braking cleanly afterwards
options.misconception: invents a contamination risk the sheet never mentions, and the quick release is already open

options.text: The chain snaps because the derailleur spring is still under tension when the wheel leaves
options.misconception: supplies a chain tension the sheet never describes anywhere in its three steps

options.text: The wheel is no longer held once the nuts are loose, and it can drop as it clears the dropouts
The axle nuts strip their threads because loosening them by hand cannot turn them far enough
options.misconception: reads the hand loosening as a risk, when loosening by hand removes the tool damage instead

questions.explanation: Trace what each step removes before the last one begins. Step 2 releases the brake, and step 3 loosens the nuts, and those are the two things holding a bicycle wheel in the frame. Once both are done the wheel is supported by nothing but the reader's grip, and lift it out of the dropouts is the moment it becomes free, so the exposure exists in that step and nowhere earlier. A safety note here would sit before or inside step 3. The other three options name hazards the sheet never introduces: no chain tension, no oil, and hand loosening is the step's own answer to a nut-stripping risk.
questions.hint: List what the first two steps have let go of by the time step 3 begins.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: Recovery when a step fails
questions.learningObjective: supply the elements a one-line retry instruction leaves out
questions.stem: A stain removal guide says of a dried mark: 'If it does not lift, repeat the treatment.' Which change turns that line into usable instruction?

options.text: Delete the sentence, because a treatment applied often enough will lift any mark in the end
options.misconception: assumes persistence alone will remove a mark that the guide itself treats as resistant

options.text: Rewrite it as repeat until the mark lifts, which turns an open-ended loop into a definite goal
options.misconception: adds a stopping word without saying what failure looks like or how many attempts are safe

options.text: Attach a photograph of the treated fabric after each attempt, so the reader can see the change
options.misconception: supplies an image where the real gap is that nothing tells the reader what a failed attempt looks like

options.text: Say what to check before repeating, how many times to try, and when trying stops helping

questions.explanation: A retry line has to carry three things or it is not an instruction: a diagnosis, because the treatment may be wrong for this mark, a limit, because a fourth application may set a stain or weaken a fabric, and a stop rule, because the reader needs to know when the mark is no longer responding rather than when patience has run out. The sentence as printed carries none of them; it only asserts that a second try is available. Repeating until the mark lifts is the same line with a mood of confidence added, and a photograph shows change but not the point at which to abandon the method, so neither repair answers the diagnosis and the limit.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would do differently the second time, and when they should stop.

questions.topic: Where a safety warning is placed
questions.learningObjective: judge what a warning's position costs the reader

stimulus.body: 1. Unplug the heater before cleaning it. 2. Remove the back panel and set it aside. 3. Vacuum the coils and the fan housing. WARNING: Do not put the heater back into the socket while the panel is off. 4. Replace the back panel. 5. Plug the heater in and test it.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A cleaning guide reads: '1. Unplug the heater before cleaning it. 2. Remove the back panel and set it aside. 3. Vacuum the coils and the fan housing. WARNING: Do not put the heater back into the socket while the panel is off. 4. Replace the back panel. 5. Plug the heater in and test it.' What does the warning's position cost the reader?

options.text: The panel is off in step 2, so the reader has created the hazard before the warning arrives
The warning sits after the last numbered step, so a reader who finishes at step 5 never meets it
options.misconception: puts the warning after the guide's last line, when it is printed between steps 3 and 4

options.text: The warning repeats step 1, so the guide spends a line saying that the heater is unplugged
options.misconception: confuses unplugging the flex with re-enclosing a live heater, which the warning forbids

options.text: The warning is printed among numbered steps, so a reader will take it for one more operation
options.misconception: reads a labelled warning as an instruction, when a heading and caps already mark it as standing advice

questions.explanation: A warning earns its place by standing between the reader and the act it forbids, so its position is part of its meaning. Here the hazard is created in step 2, when the back panel comes off and the live elements are exposed, and the warning that names it is printed after step 3. For two steps the reader is working inside the hazard the sheet has not yet described, and the first instruction that would trigger it, plug the heater in at step 5, is far enough away that the connection may be made. Moving the warning to sit with step 2, or repeating it at step 4, would restore the ordering the reader needs.
questions.hint: Find the step that creates the danger and compare its number with the warning's.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: One step given two different values
questions.learningObjective: report a guide's own inconsistency accurately

stimulus.body: Section 2, preparing the joint: Spread the adhesive and bring the parts together. Hold the joint clamped for four hours before moving it. Section 5, finishing: Once the adhesive has held for two hours the joint can be sanded flush. Allow longer in cold conditions.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A two-part manual says: 'Section 2, preparing the joint: Spread the adhesive and bring the parts together. Hold the joint clamped for four hours before moving it. Section 5, finishing: Once the adhesive has held for two hours the joint can be sanded flush. Allow longer in cold conditions.' Which sentence reports the manual's position accurately?

options.text: The two-hour figure is conditional on cold conditions, so the two sections do not actually disagree
options.misconception: makes the cold condition govern the two hours, when the manual offers it only as a reason to allow longer

options.text: Sections 2 and 5 give two holding times for the same adhesive, so a reader cannot tell which one governs
Four hours applies to clamping and two hours to sanding, so each activity has its own time
options.misconception: splits one adhesive into two duties, though both figures are times the same adhesive has held

options.text: Section 5 replaces Section 2 because a later section gives the manual's most recent figure
options.misconception: reads document order as revision history, which the manual nowhere claims

questions.explanation: Both figures describe how long the same adhesive has held, so they are two answers to one question and cannot both be the manual's advice. Section 2 says four hours before moving the joint; Section 5 says two hours before sanding. Nothing in either section scopes its figure to a different job, to a different material, or to a different part, and the one qualifier supplied, allow longer in cold conditions, makes the two-hour figure a starting point rather than a way of resolving the conflict. Reporting a source means reporting the inconsistency as it stands; assigning the numbers to separate jobs, or inventing a revision order between sections, would give the manual a consistency it does not have.
questions.hint: Ask whether both figures answer the same question about the same material.

questions.stem: A maintenance card reads: '4. The tray is drained overnight. 5. The lining is checked for damage and replaced if needed. 6. Power is restored at the isolator.' First name what the reader cannot settle, then choose the repair that keeps every action.

options.text: What drained means is unresolved, so the repair should define the drainage method for the reader
options.misconception: treats an ordinary passive verb as an ambiguity, when the missing thing is who acts

options.text: When the lining is checked is unstated, so the repair should move step 5 to follow step 6
options.misconception: reorders steps to solve a missing agent, which reordering cannot supply

options.text: Who checks the lining is never named, so the repair gives that person a name and leaves the rest alone
Where the isolator stands is not given, so the repair should add a description of its location
options.misconception: claims a missing fact about a place the card has already named

questions.topic: A modifier that could take two scopes
questions.learningObjective: locate the phrase in a step that admits more than one attachment
questions.stem: A recipe step reads: 'Fold the butter into the flour, turning the bowl as you go, until the mixture looks like breadcrumbs.' Which part of the step is left open?

options.text: How long the whole mixing should take, since breadcrumbs do not name a duration
options.misconception: asks for a time the step replaces with a test the reader can make, namely the look of the mixture

options.text: How much butter the recipe calls for, since the step names the butter without giving a weight
options.misconception: wants a quantity inside a step, when quantities belong in the ingredient list the card already has

options.text: What colour the crumbs should be, since breadcrumbs are a shape and not a shade
options.misconception: asks for a visual check the step already supplies by naming a texture

options.text: Whether turning the bowl is one more mixing movement or a way of steadying the bowl

questions.explanation: Turning the bowl is a phrase that can belong to the hand movement or to the bowl, and the two readings ask for different work: one adds a second motion to the folding, the other is advice about grip. A step that mixes a named action into a supporting clause leaves the reader to pick, and picking wrongly is harmless here but costly in a step where the motion itself is the point. The other three options treat the step as incomplete when it is not: it gives a stop test rather than a time, and the quantity and the shade were never this step's job.
questions.hint: Ask whether the reader's hands or the bowl are what turns.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: Moves in the opening of a procedure
questions.learningObjective: order the elements that make a guide's opening usable
questions.stem: A writer is drafting the opening of a repair guide aimed at people who have never done the job. Put the four moves in the order that opening needs.

options.text: Say what the finished job will be, so a reader can tell at once whether this is their procedure
List the tools and parts, so nothing turns out to be missing in the middle of the work
State the condition the machine must be in, which rules out starting on a job that needs a different guide
Give the time the job takes, so the reader can choose when to begin it

questions.explanation: The opening answers four questions in the order a reader meets them. First, what will be true at the end, since a reader who cannot tell whether this is their job will not start. Second, what must be true before they start, which is the step that saves a reader from arriving at step 6 with a machine that needed a different procedure. Third, what must be on the table, so a missing part is discovered at the start rather than halfway through with the machine in pieces. Fourth, how long it takes, which affects when to begin and can only be estimated once the earlier three are settled. Tools before the starting condition would leave a reader who cannot even begin reading about shopping, and time before the goal would be a number attached to nothing.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader needs to know, in order, before they can start and before they can plan.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: The check a step needs before it is done
questions.learningObjective: say what makes a fitting step verifiable while it is being done
questions.stem: A guide's step 4 reads: 'Fit the belt and tension it.' What must that step supply for a reader to know the tension is right?

options.text: The maker of the belt, since tension figures are quoted by the manufacturer and not by the guide
options.misconception: supplies a purchasing detail where the missing thing is a check the reader can perform unaided

options.text: A test the reader makes during fitting, such as a stated span that has not moved or a stated deflection
The number of turns the adjuster takes, so that the result is repeatable on the next belt
options.misconception: counts turns as the verification, when turns differ once the belt has settled

options.text: A diagram of the adjuster, so the reader can see which of the two slots takes the belt
options.misconception: adds a picture of the mechanism where the gap is a way of testing tension

questions.explanation: Tension is a condition, not an action, and an action that produces a condition is only finished when the reader can see the condition. Fit the belt and tension it tells the reader what to do and stops at the point where two outcomes, correct and slipping, look identical from the outside. A verification has to be available at the fitting: a stated span on two pulleys that must not change, a stated deflection pressed at the middle of the belt, a mark that must stay aligned. Turns of an adjuster, a maker's name, and a drawing of the slot all describe the mechanism rather than the result, so a reader using them would still not know whether the belt holds.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader could look at immediately after fitting and before letting go.

options.misconception: claims a missing isolation step, when the guide's own gap is an obstacle standing in front of step 7

options.text: The side cover is described by its bolt count, which gives no clue what the cover looks like

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A quantity that cannot be measured as written
questions.learningObjective: judge whether a stated amount can be carried out twice

stimulus.body: Warm the oil in a shallow pan. Fry the pieces until they float. Turn them once, then drain on kitchen paper and salt well.
stimulus.license: CC0-1.0 public domain dedication; prose written for this bank

questions.stem: A card for frying dough pieces reads: 'Warm the oil in a shallow pan. Fry the pieces until they float. Turn them once, then drain on kitchen paper and salt well.' Which instruction cannot be followed the same way twice?

options.text: Drain on kitchen paper, because paper is not a stated surface with a stated grade
options.misconception: demands a specification where the card names a surface the reader can recognise

options.text: Fry the pieces until they float, because floating depends on the density of the oil and not the dough
options.misconception: mislabels a test the card gives on purpose, since floating is exactly the sign it chose

options.text: Turn them once, since a single turn cannot be timed and the pieces need even heat on both sides
options.misconception: objects to a countable action that needs no timing to be performed

options.text: Salt well, since the card gives no amount, no container and no basis for deciding what well means

questions.explanation: A quantity is usable if two readers would put about the same amount on the same plate, and well fails that test in three ways at once: no volume, no container to measure it in, and no baseline such as a stated weight or a per-piece figure. The other three instructions all pass. Kitchen paper names a surface every reader can find, floating is a test rather than a measurement and is a deliberate choice because it needs no timer, and turn them once is a countable action whose result is visible. The distinction matters because a card may legitimately judge by eye, as with the crumbs, but it has to say so; well reads as a measurement and supplies none.
questions.hint: Ask which word would have to be measured, and with what, before the instruction could be repeated.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: A ratio that leaves the final amount open
questions.learningObjective: state what a dilution figure fixes and what it does not
questions.stem: A label on a concentrate reads: 'Dilute 1 part concentrate to 10 parts water before use.' Which statement about that label is accurate?

options.text: It fixes the proportion between the two liquids but not how much mixture to make
It fixes the final volume, because eleven parts of liquid is a volume a reader can measure out
options.misconception: treats a ratio of parts as a quantity of mixture to be produced

options.text: It is unusable, because a ratio can only be given for solids and never for liquids
options.misconception: denies a form of expression that labels for liquids use as a matter of course

options.text: It fixes the order of addition, because the label names the concentrate before the water
options.misconception: reads the order of the words as an instruction about which liquid goes in first

questions.explanation: A parts ratio is a relation between two amounts, so it answers the question how strong, and it leaves open the question how much. One part to ten parts works equally well in a thimbleful and in a bucket, which is convenient when the amount depends on the job and a fault when the reader has no other clue, because a first-time user will pour the largest amount the vessel holds. Eleven parts is a ratio result, not a volume; nothing on the label commits anyone to eleven of anything. Naming the concentrate first reads as tidiness, not as an order of pouring, and ratios describe liquids perfectly well, which is what labels on every dilutable product rely on.
questions.hint: Ask what the ratio would still need before a reader could mix a known amount.

questions.learningObjective: decide where a shared limit must appear so it reaches every step it governs

questions.stem: A guide prints one note above a run of seven mixing steps: 'For all steps in this section, do not exceed 40 degrees or the mixture will set too hard to spread.' Which problem follows from that placement?

options.text: One note for seven steps is too little text, so readers will skim past it however it is worded
options.misconception: blames brevity, when a single sentence can carry a limit to any number of steps

options.text: The note gives a number but not the instrument, so the reader cannot tell how 40 degrees is measured
options.misconception: singles out the instrument, when the real fault is the note's distance from the steps it governs

options.text: The limit is separated from the steps by a page break, so a reader on the later page will not see it
The note belongs after the first step instead, because a limit only means something once work has begun
options.misconception: moves a limit later, which is the opposite of what a governing note needs

questions.explanation: A note that governs several steps has to stay in view of all of them, and a numbered run that fills a page will not, because readers locate steps by number and read from the step down. Printing the limit above the run means the pages that carry steps five to seven hold no trace of it, and the damage the note prevents, a mixture that sets before it can be spread, is exactly the damage a reader on the last page cannot detect early. The instrument question is real but secondary, and a short note is not a weak note; the position is what decides whether the constraint is present when the step is read.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader who has turned the page will have in front of them.

The document addresses one reader, and the two headings only name two stages of the same visit

No: replace the switch, then test again. Yes: go to node 2. Node 2: Check the bulb. No: fit a new bulb, then test again. Yes: go to node 3. Node 3: Check the plug is seated in the wall. No: reseat the plug, then test again. Yes: go to node 4. Node 4: Test at a different wall socket. No: stop, the fault is in the supply. Yes: stop, the fault is in the lamp.' What is wrong with the order of this tree?

options.misconception: counts the branches at the last node, when each branch carries its own stated verdict

options.misconception: reads a retest after a repair as a loop, when each repair ends in a fresh test at the same lamp

options.text: The tree checks the parts before the supply, so a lamp with a dead socket is sent to a part that was never faulty
options.misconception: objects to the order of cheap and expensive repairs, which is an order of cost and not of possibility

The tree asks that question first and supplies the two conditions for asking it two nodes later, so a reader following it in order reaches node 1 with nothing to observe. The cheapest useful test here is the one a reader can make unaided, which is why the plug comes before the bulb and the switch last. Node 4's two endings are labelled, and a retest after a repair is a new test rather than a loop.
questions.hint: For each node, ask what the reader must already have done before its test means anything.

options.misconception: treats a reason as an invitation, when it fixes what the reader should expect to happen

questions.stem: A maker's guide gives a service table with a heading 'every 12 months or 8,000 kilometres, whichever comes first'. Put the four moves in the order that interval needs before the table is usable.

State what the interval measures, whether it is time, distance, or the earlier of the two
Name the jobs the interval covers, so a reader can see which items the service includes
Give the limits that count as done, so a reader can tell a completed job from a partial one

questions.explanation: An interval is only usable once four things are settled, and they settle in this order. First the trigger, so the reader can work out when the service falls due, and a heading that says time or distance or whichever comes first has to be read as a rule about the two together. Then the contents, so a reader knows what the visit is for. Then the acceptance condition, because a service that lists jobs without saying what counts as finished leaves the owner unable to check the work. Last the consequence of missing it, which is the only part that lets a reader weigh the interval against other spending. Contents before the trigger would leave a list that cannot be scheduled, and the consequence before the trigger would be advice attached to a date nobody can compute.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader needs in order to calendar the job, to know its scope, to check it, and to judge it.

options.misconception: calls them equivalent, when the manual states an exception the datasheet does not

options.text: The datasheet settles the question, since it is the maker's own summary of the terms
options.misconception: invents a hierarchy between two documents that never claim one over the other

options.text: Neither can be relied on, since two different statements of one warranty cannot both be correct
options.misconception: condemns both, where what differs is a condition and not the fact of opening

options.text: The manual adds a condition the datasheet does not have, so the boundary differs between the two

The datasheet makes opening the unit a plain end of cover; the manual makes it the end of cover only if the original seal is broken, so a unit opened and correctly resealed is covered by one document and not by the other. A condition has been added, which is a difference in scope rather than a contradiction about the fact of opening, so both can be true statements of their own terms. How long slowly should last, so the repair should replace the pace with a figure in seconds

options.text: Which washer fits, so the repair should name the part together with its size
options.misconception: asks for a part detail, when the gap is what follows the last check

options.text: Whether the tap goes back before the water is on, so the repair should reverse the last two actions
options.misconception: supplies an ordering fault the passage does not contain

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: Order of the parts of a fault report
questions.learningObjective: order the elements of a report another person can act on
questions.stem: A support team wants every fault report usable by a colleague who cannot ring the writer. Put the four moves in the order that report needs.

options.text: Say what was seen or heard, in plain words, so the colleague can match it against known faults
Say what has already been tried, so the colleague does not spend the call repeating it
Say what the writer thinks is happening, kept apart from what was actually observed
Say what the machine was doing when the fault appeared, so the fault has a setting to be judged in

questions.explanation: The report is read by someone matching it against faults they already know, so it opens with what was observed: the sound, the smell, the message on the screen, in the writer's words rather than in a diagnosis. The setting comes next, because the same observation means different things cold and under load. What has been tried comes third, and it is the field that stops a support call from repeating work the writer has already done. The writer's theory comes last and stays separated, because it is the one part of the report a colleague cannot check and the part most likely to mislead a search. Putting the theory first would have the colleague confirming a guess instead of reading an observation.
questions.hint: Ask what the colleague needs to identify the fault, then what they need to act on it.

options.misconception: counts repetition as emphasis, when the note names no rule at all

options.text: It has made step 4 conditional, so the bracket goes on only if it can be made square
options.misconception: invents a condition, when the note asserts a rule and sets no test

options.text: Nothing beyond a second mention of step 4, because the requirement itself is still not stated
It has sent the reader back to the step that already explains squareness
options.misconception: believes step 4 explains squareness, which is the very requirement the note omits

questions.explanation: Read the note for information rather than for emphasis. The rule is that the bracket must be fitted square; the note says the bracket must be fitted square, as in step 4, which adds a pointer and no content. If step 4 had already said how to check squareness, the note would be a signpost; as printed, the requirement is asserted in both places and explained in neither, so a reader who wanted to know what square means is sent to a step that does not say. Emphasis is a real effect of repetition, but it cannot substitute for the one thing the guide has not supplied.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader learns from the note that step 4 did not already contain.

options.misconception: accepts the durability claim as part of the same sentence

options.misconception: reads a premise the passage may not have established as a claim made by it

options.text: That the seal was tested, since the sentence mentions a sound seal without saying how
options.misconception: goes after an untested part, where the claim is about endurance

options.text: That the unit will hold full pressure indefinitely, which no service step can establish

questions.stem: A clamping guide reads: '4. Tighten the clamp until the parts stop moving. 5. Leave the joint under clamp for a few minutes, then check that it has held and that the faces are still in contact.' Which figure must the reader supply for themselves?

options.text: How long the clamp stays on, since a few minutes does not fix when the check can mean anything
How tightly the clamp is tightened, because stop moving is a test of motion and not a figure
options.misconception: reads step 4 as the gap, when the untimed wait is what step 5 introduces

options.text: How the joint is checked, since held is not a measurement a reader can take
options.misconception: objects to an ordinary test word when the missing figure is a length of time

options.text: What is being stopped, since parts is the only loose noun in the whole pair of steps
options.misconception: picks a question of reference that the guide's own nouns largely settle

It is a hedge that leaves the interval to the reader's own sense of how long minutes are, and the two plausible readings, a short wait to test that nothing moves, and a longer one to let the adhesive set, would be carried out differently. questions.hint: Ask how long the joint must be clamped before the reader's check tells them anything.

questions.topic: A procedure with no stated goal
questions.learningObjective: supply the element a step list is missing at its head
questions.stem: A card runs: '1. Remove the lid. 2. Lift out the filter. 3. Rinse the filter under the tap. 4. Dry the filter. 5. Refit the filter and the lid.' It never says what the reader is trying to achieve. What does it most need?

options.text: More steps, since a longer list makes the purpose clearer to a reader working quickly
options.misconception: believes quantity communicates an aim, which it cannot do

options.text: A line stating the finished result, so a step can be judged by whether it moves towards it
A title on each step, since a heading can state what the step beneath it is for
options.misconception: confuses the title of a step with the purpose of the job

options.text: A list of the tools, since the equipment shows the reader what they are working towards
options.misconception: supplies equipment where the missing thing is a destination

questions.explanation: Steps are means, and a list of means with no stated end leaves a reader unable to tell when to stop, unable to tell whether a step has been done well, and unable to notice that the list is going in the wrong direction. Headings on individual steps are useful but local, and a tool list describes equipment rather than purpose. More steps would make the absence harder to see, not easier.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader is meant to have at the end, and where the card says so.

options.misconception: asks for identification, when the open item is the state the unit was left in

options.text: Why the third connection was left alone, which cannot be reached does not begin to say
options.misconception: supplies a reason the entry does give, and misses the untested state

options.text: How the unit was proved serviceable, since powered up does not say what was done to test it

options.misconception: asks for timings, when nothing in the record depends on them

Box 1: Lay one frame A flat. Box 2: Bolt rail D between the two frames A, using bag 1. Box 3: Fix seat panel B across the frames. Box 4: Screw the four legs C into the sockets under B. questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: What a good warning contains
questions.learningObjective: select what a warning has to supply to change a reader's action
questions.stem: A maker prints warnings beside the steps of a machine's manual. Which three things must such a warning supply if it is to change what a reader does?

options.text: The act to be avoided, in words narrow enough to recognise while working
What to do if it has already happened, so the reader is not left improvising
The name of the engineer who approved the machine's design
options.misconception: asks for an approval record, which no reader can act on at the machine

options.text: The date on which the warning was added to later printings
options.misconception: asks for a revision date, which tells a reader nothing about the danger

options.text: The condition in which the danger appears, so a reader can tell whether they are in it

questions.explanation: A warning has to do three jobs, and each of the three is a different moment. The condition says when the danger is present, so a reader can recognise that they are in it rather than reading past it as routine. The act says what not to do, narrowly enough to be recognised in the middle of a task, because a warning against carelessness cannot be obeyed. The recovery says what to do afterwards, which is the part manuals most often omit and the part a reader needs most, since by the time they have read a warning about a hazard the hazard has usually already happened. An approval record and a revision date tell a reader nothing they can do at the machine.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader needs to know before, during, and after the moment of danger.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.topic: The draft with a sentence cut out
questions.learningObjective: supply a missing procedural sentence that its position in the sequence requires
questions.stem: The draft of a jointing guide reads: '1. Heat the joint along its length, moving the flame steadily. 2. [a sentence is missing here] 3. Slide the two pieces home and clamp them. Remove the clamp after the glue has set.' In three or four sentences, say what the missing sentence has to do and write it.

answer.exemplar: The gap sits between heating the joint and assembling the pieces, so the missing sentence has to do one job: tell the reader how to tell that the joint is ready. A description of the heating is no use, because step 1 has already given it, and a warning about the flame is a safety matter rather than the missing content. What the sentence needs is a test the reader can make at that point, and a heat test is what fits. Written as the step: 'Push the joint with a thumbnail. When the surface still feels soft and springs back only slowly, the joint is ready to assemble.' That gives step 3 a condition to act on, and it costs the reader nothing they cannot do with a hand already at the joint.

questions.explanation: A missing sentence in a procedure is not a gap in the writing but a missing unit of work, and its content is decided by the two steps around it. Step 1 applies heat and step 3 assembles, so the sentence between them has to bridge the two: it must let the reader decide, at the joint and in the moment, that the first step has done enough. That is a readiness test, and the test has to be one the reader can perform with what is at hand. Naming a temperature instead would be equally useful where a thermometer is available, which shows that the requirement is a test the reader can make rather than a particular instrument. Any answer that restates the heating, that adds a safety caution, or that puts the readiness test somewhere else has not filled this particular gap.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader must be able to establish, and when, before step 3 is safe to do.

questions.stem: A maker's note runs: 'The machine is fitted with a guard over the belt drive. Guards cost little to fit and stop the belt touching the operator's hand. Every machine of this class we have examined came with one, and none of them has ever been involved in an injury. That is why we regard the guard as the safest part of the design.' What is the strongest objection to the last sentence?

options.text: Every machine examined came with one, which shows only what this class of machine was sold with
options.misconception: attacks what the sample was made of rather than what was observed about it

options.text: Guards cost little, which is a claim about price and bears on nothing to do with safety
options.misconception: calls an irrelevant fact irrelevant, which does not damage a safety claim

options.text: The last sentence ranks one part against a whole design, and the machine's safety was never tested
options.misconception: supposes a claim about the design that the sentence does not make about the guard

options.text: None was ever involved in an injury, which may say as much about reporting as about guards

questions.explanation: The last sentence rests its rank on a record of no injuries, and the force of that record depends on how complete it is. The note says none of the machines examined has ever been involved in an injury, which is a statement about what has been noticed and reported as well as about what happened, and a reader is entitled to ask how an injury reaches the record at all, how many machines the note examined, and over what period. That is an objection to the inference rather than to the note's facts, and it is the strongest because the note offers no other evidence for the ranking. The cost and the sample's composition are weaker: one is beside the point and the other concerns what was fitted rather than what happened.
questions.hint: Ask what else the note's no-injury record would be true of, if the guards were not there.
